title: Returns
why_now: The selected price series needs a comparable change measure before volatility, momentum, or regression can be interpreted.
background: Returns turn a price path into scale-aware observations.
intuition: A return asks how much the value changed relative to where it started.
limitations: Historical returns do not guarantee future returns.

derivations.operation: compare the change with the starting level
derivations.reason: A scale-free change is comparable across assets.

misconceptions.claim: A positive return means the next return will also be positive.
misconceptions.correction: A return describes the observed interval and is not a forecast.

title: Volatility
why_now: The current research sample uses realized volatility to describe how unstable recent returns have been.
background: Variance measures dispersion around a mean; its square root preserves the original units.
intuition: Volatility is the typical size of a return surprise in the observed sample.
assumptions: The return observations are comparable and the sample window is declared.
limitations: Historical realized volatility is not a guarantee of future volatility.

derivations.reason: Squared deviations prevent positive and negative surprises from cancelling.

proofs.strategy: The square root of a sum of squared deviations cannot be negative.

misconceptions.claim: High volatility means the asset must lose money.

exercises.prompt: Change the return window and observe the sample standard deviation.

title: OLS Regression and Beta
why_now: The selected regression result contains a beta estimate, so the learner needs to see what the slope means and how it was fitted.
background: Least squares solves the problem of choosing a line whose residuals are small in squared aggregate.
intuition: OLS projects the observed outcome vector onto the space explained by the predictors.
assumptions: Observations are aligned and available at the research timestamp.
limitations: A fitted beta is an estimate for the sample, not a causal guarantee or forecast.

equations.meaning: fitted return from intercept and factor exposure
slope as covariance divided by factor variance

derivations.reason: Squaring makes the total error differentiable and penalizes larger misses more.

derivations.operation: solve the normal equation for the slope
derivations.reason: The derivative of the objective is zero at the least-squares stationary point.

proofs.statement: The fitted line is stationary for the squared-error objective.
proofs.strategy: Differentiate the objective and set the normal-equation gradient to zero.

misconceptions.claim: A significant beta proves the factor causes the return.
misconceptions.correction: Regression association depends on design, assumptions, and omitted variables.

exercises.prompt: Move one point and inspect the slope and residuals.

title: Sharpe Ratio
why_now: The current paper strategy has an annualized return and volatility; the ratio compares excess return with the variability paid to earn it.
background: Risk-adjusted performance asks whether average excess return is large relative to its sample dispersion.
intuition: Sharpe is a scale-normalized comparison, not a promise of future performance.
assumptions: The return and risk-free series use the same period and units.
limitations: Estimation error, non-normality, and regime change can make a historical Sharpe unstable.

equations.meaning: mean excess return divided by volatility

derivations.operation: subtract the risk-free return before scaling by risk
derivations.reason: Only return above the baseline is treated as compensation for risk.

proofs.statement: Sharpe is dimensionless when numerator and denominator use matching return units.
proofs.strategy: Both terms are returns, so their quotient cancels units.

misconceptions.claim: The highest historical Sharpe is automatically the best strategy.
misconceptions.correction: Selection, OOS evidence, costs, and uncertainty must be reviewed together.

exercises.prompt: Increase volatility while holding excess return fixed and observe the ratio.

title: Momentum
why_now: The current StrategySpec ranks assets by a declared lookback return, so the learner should see how the window changes the feature and strategy signal.
background: Momentum research studies whether recent relative performance contains information about later cross-sectional outcomes.
intuition: Momentum is a rule for measuring recent movement, not a law that prices must continue rising.
assumptions: Prices are aligned, split-adjusted, and available at the feature timestamp.
limitations: Costs, turnover, crowding, regime change, and look-ahead can erase a historical effect.

equations.meaning: lookback return used as a momentum feature

derivations.operation: divide current price by lookback price
derivations.reason: The ratio makes the movement comparable across price levels.

proofs.statement: The feature is invariant to a common positive price unit scale.
proofs.strategy: Multiplying both prices by the same positive constant cancels in the ratio.

misconceptions.claim: Momentum is a guarantee that winners keep winning.
misconceptions.correction: It is a historical feature whose performance is sensitive to sample, costs, and regime.

exercises.prompt: Change the lookback window and inspect the feature value.

title: Out-of-Sample and Overfitting
why_now: The research result is about to be interpreted, so the learner must distinguish in-sample fit from evidence on untouched observations.
background: Model selection can memorize a sample; an OOS split tests whether a declared process survives data it did not optimize against.
intuition: OOS is a held-back reality check, not a guarantee of future performance.
assumptions: The split and selection process are declared before the final OOS read.
limitations: One historical split can still be unrepresentative and does not remove all multiple-testing risk.

equations.meaning: declared observations partitioned into train and OOS

derivations.operation: freeze the OOS portion before selection
derivations.reason: Untouched observations reduce (but do not eliminate) selection bias.
assumptions: No future information enters training or selection

proofs.statement: A declared OOS set is not used to fit the selected parameters.
proofs.strategy: The workflow contract separates the data scopes before evaluation.

misconceptions.claim: A positive OOS result proves the strategy will work next year.
misconceptions.correction: It is historical evidence under one declared split and remains uncertain.

exercises.prompt: Change the train ratio and inspect which observations remain OOS.
